<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Broadcast Rights  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Broadcast rights consist principally of rights to broadcast syndicated programs, sports and feature films and are stated at the lower of cost or estimated net
realizable value. The total cost of these rights is recorded as an asset and a liability when the program becomes available for broadcast. Syndicated program rights that have limited showings are
generally amortized using an accelerated method as programs are aired. Sports and feature film rights are amortized using the straight-line method. The current portion of broadcast rights
represents those rights available for broadcast that are expected to be amortized in the succeeding year. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, the Company had broadcast rights assets of
$669&nbsp;million and $652&nbsp;million, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company maintains an allowance for programming that is not expected to be aired by the end of the contract period. This allowance for excess programming inventory is based on a
program-by-program review of the Company's five-year broadcast plans and historical write-off trends. The total reserve balance at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005
and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004 was $4&nbsp;million and $5&nbsp;million, respectively. Actual write-offs in 2005 and 2004 were $1&nbsp;million and $12&nbsp;million, respectively. Future
write-offs can vary based on changes in consumer viewing trends and the availability and costs of other programming. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company periodically reviews goodwill and certain intangible assets no longer being amortized for impairment in accordance with FAS No.&nbsp;142, "Goodwill
and Other Intangible Assets." Under FAS No.&nbsp;142, the impairment review of goodwill and other intangible assets not subject to amortization must be based generally on fair values. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
estimated fair value of the reporting units to which goodwill is allocated is determined using multiples of operating cash flows for purposes of analyzing goodwill for impairment.
The estimated fair values of other assets subject to the annual impairment review, which include newspaper mastheads and FCC licenses, are calculated based on projected future discounted cash flow
analyses. The development of market multiples and cash flow projections used in the analyses requires the use of assumptions, including assumptions regarding revenue and market growth. The analyses
use discount rates based on specific economic factors in the publishing and broadcasting industries. These assumptions reflect the Company's best estimates, but these items involve inherent
uncertainties based on market conditions generally outside of the Company's control. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
the fourth quarter of 2004, the Company elected to early adopt the provisions of the Financial Accounting Standards Board's Emerging Issues Task Force Topic
No.&nbsp;D-108, which requires the use of a direct valuation method for valuing intangible assets, such as FCC licenses, and reviewing them for impairment. Historically, the Company had
been using a residual valuation method to review its FCC licenses for impairment each year. A direct valuation method generally results in a lower valuation than </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>32</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>
<!-- ZEQ.=6,SEQ=35,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=503916,FOLIO='32',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]DM1126A.;17',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:06' -->
<A NAME="page_dm1126_1_33"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>does
a residual valuation method. The Company performed an impairment review of its FCC licenses for the year ended Dec.&nbsp;28, 2003 using a residual method. No impairments were required as a
result of the analyses performed in 2003. The effect of changing to a direct valuation method for the 2004 FCC licenses impairment review was a pretax charge of $29&nbsp;million ($18&nbsp;million
after-tax). The charge was recorded in the fourth quarter of 2004 as a cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle in the consolidated statements of income. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Upon
the adoption of FAS No.&nbsp;142 at the beginning of fiscal 2002, the Company treated the intangible assets associated with network affiliation agreements as having indefinite
lives and stopped recording amortization expense on these assets. In December&nbsp;2003, the staff of the Securities and Exchange Commission provided guidance regarding their accounting position in
this area indicating that network affiliation agreements should be amortized. As a result, the Company began amortizing these assets in the fourth quarter of 2003 using a 40-year life. The
Company believes the 40-year life is representative of the remaining expected useful life of the network affiliation intangibles. The provisions of FAS No.&nbsp;142 required the Company
to perform an impairment analysis at the time of a change in the estimated useful life of an intangible asset which was previously not being amortized. No adjustment to the network affiliation
intangible assets was required as a result of this impairment review performed in the fourth quarter of 2003. Beginning in 2004, the Company no longer performs an annual test of the impairment of its
network affiliation agreements under FAS No.&nbsp;142, but will perform an impairment test if indicators of impairment are present, as required by FAS No.&nbsp;144, "Accounting for the Impairment
or Disposal of Long-Lived Assets." </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Self-Insurance Liabilities  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company self-insures for certain medical and disability benefits, workers' compensation costs and automobile and general liability claims. The
recorded liabilities for self-insured risks are calculated using actuarial methods and are not discounted. The liabilities include amounts for actual claims, claim growth and claims
incurred but not reported. Actual experience, including claim frequency and severity as well as health care inflation, could result in different liabilities than the amounts currently recorded. The
recorded liabilities for self-insured risks totaled $113&nbsp;million and $106&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Accounts Receivable Allowances  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company's accounts receivable are primarily due from advertisers. Credit is extended based on an evaluation of a customer's financial condition and generally
collateral is not required. The Company maintains an allowance for uncollectible accounts, rebates and volume discounts. This allowance is determined based on historical write-off
experience and any known specific collectibility exposures. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, the Company's allowance for accounts receivable was $43&nbsp;million and
$50&nbsp;million, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Stock-Based Compensation  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company accounts for its stock-based compensation plans in accordance with Accounting Principles Board ("APB") Opinion No.&nbsp;25 and related
interpretations. Under APB No.&nbsp;25, no compensation expense is recorded because the exercise price of employee stock options equals the market price of the underlying stock on the date of grant. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
June&nbsp;24, 2005, the Company accelerated the vesting of certain stock options granted on Feb.&nbsp;11, 2003 and Feb.&nbsp;10, 2004, totaling 2.4&nbsp;million in each year.
Unvested stock options awarded to the then current executive officers of the Company on these grant dates, which aggregated 0.8&nbsp;million and 0.6&nbsp;million, respectively, were not
accelerated at that time. On Dec.&nbsp;16, 2005, the Company accelerated the vesting of all stock options granted on Feb.&nbsp;8, 2005, totaling 3.5&nbsp;million. Also, on Dec.&nbsp;16, 2005,
the Company accelerated the remaining unvested stock options granted to the current executive officers of the Company on Feb.&nbsp;11, 2003 and Feb.&nbsp;10, 2004, totaling 0.4&nbsp;million in
both years. All other terms and conditions of the stock option grants remain unchanged. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
accordance with APB No.&nbsp;25 and related interpretations, the acceleration of vesting of these stock options did not require accounting recognition in the Company's income
statement. The exercise prices of the 2003, 2004 and 2005 grants were $45.90, $52.05 and $40.59, respectively, and the Company's closing stock prices on the June&nbsp;24, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;16,
2005 dates of acceleration were $35.64 and $30.80, respectively. The impact of the accelerated vesting was to increase pro forma stock-based compensation by $82&nbsp;million, or $50&nbsp;million
net of tax, in 2005. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
accelerated vesting of these stock options was one of several actions the Company has recently taken to reduce stock-based compensation expense that will be recorded in future years
with the adoption of Financial Accounting Standard ("FAS") No.&nbsp;123R (see discussion below). Over the last two years, the Company has reduced the number of stock options granted by approximately
45%. Also, beginning in 2004, option grants have 8-year terms, down from 10&nbsp;years for grants in previous years, and do not have a replacement option feature. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under
FAS No.&nbsp;123, "Accounting for Stock-Based Compensation," as amended by FAS No.&nbsp;148, compensation cost is measured at the grant date based on the estimated fair value
of the award and is recognized as compensation expense over the vesting period. For purposes of the disclosure required by FAS No.&nbsp;123, as amended by FAS No.&nbsp;148, the Company uses the
Black-Scholes option pricing model to determine the fair value of each option grant. The Black-Scholes model includes assumptions regarding dividend yields, expected volatility, expected lives and
risk-free interest rates. These </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>34</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>
<!-- ZEQ.=8,SEQ=37,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=80420,FOLIO='34',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]DM1126A.;17',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:06' -->
<A NAME="page_dm1126_1_35"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>assumptions
reflect the Company's best estimates, but these items involve inherent uncertainties based on market conditions generally outside of the control of the Company. As a result, if other
assumptions had been used in the current period, pro forma stock-based compensation, as calculated and disclosed under FAS No.&nbsp;123, could have been materially impacted. Furthermore, if the
Company uses different assumptions in future periods, share-based compensation expense could be materially impacted. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
December&nbsp;2004, the Financial Accounting Standards Board ("FASB") issued FAS No.&nbsp;123R, "Share-Based Payment." FAS No.&nbsp;123R supercedes APB No.&nbsp;25, FAS
No.&nbsp;123, as amended by FAS No.&nbsp;148, and related interpretations. Under FAS No.&nbsp;123R, compensation cost is measured at the grant date based on the estimated fair value of the award
and is required to be recognized as compensation expense over the vesting period. The Company is required to adopt the standard in the first quarter of 2006. The Company plans to use the modified
prospective application, which requires the recognition of share-
based compensation as if the provisions of the standard had been in effect since Dec.&nbsp;25, 1994 (the beginning of the Company's 1995 fiscal year). The Company expects to record approximately
$33&nbsp;million of pretax compensation expense in 2006 related to equity grants in 2006 and prior years, as well as the Company's Employee Stock Purchase Plan. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>SIGNIFICANT EVENTS</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On Jan.&nbsp;8, 2006, Newsday's six collective bargaining units voted to accept new four-year contracts that include position eliminations, work
rule improvements, lower cost retirement plans and an increase in employee health care contributions, resulting in pretax savings of approximately $7&nbsp;million in 2006 and more than
$10&nbsp;million annually thereafter. The Company expects to record one-time pretax charges of approximately $15&nbsp;million in the first quarter of 2006 related to severance and
other payments associated with the new contracts. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
Jan.&nbsp;24, 2006, the Company announced that it had reached a 10-year agreement to affiliate 16 of its television stations currently affiliated with the WB Network
(including those in New York, Los Angeles and Chicago) with a new broadcast network, The CW Network, being launched in the fall of 2006 by Warner Brothers Entertainment and CBS. The new network will
air a portion of the programming currently on the WB Network and the UPN Network, as well as new programming. The WB Network will shut down at that time. The Company will not incur any costs related
to the shutdown of The WB Network. Three of Tribune's current WB network affiliates (Philadelphia, Atlanta and Seattle) will become independent stations at that time. When regulatory approval of the
new network is received and the new affiliation agreements become effective, the Company will write-off the WB affiliation agreement intangible assets for Philadelphia, Atlanta and Seattle. This
write-off will most likely occur in the second or third quarter of 2006 and will total approximately $15&nbsp;million before taxes. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Acquisitions  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company had no significant acquisitions in 2005 and 2004. The Company completed acquisitions totaling approximately $275&nbsp;million in 2003 for cash and
other consideration, including the value of the Denver radio station group assets that were divested in an exchange transaction during 2003. The results of the acquired companies are included in the
consolidated statements of income since their respective dates of acquisition. None of these acquisitions were material in relation to the Company's consolidated financial statements. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
March&nbsp;21, 2003, the Company acquired the stock of KPLR-TV, St.&nbsp;Louis, and the assets of KWBP-TV, Portland, Ore., from ACME Communications for a
total of $275&nbsp;million. The Company acquired the stock of KPLR-TV for $200&nbsp;million in cash. The acquisition of the assets of KWBP-TV was structured as a
like-kind asset
exchange for income tax purposes. It was funded with the remaining assets of the Denver radio station group (KKHK-FM, now known as KQMT-FM) with an estimated fair market value
of $55&nbsp;million, plus $20&nbsp;million in cash. The Company allocated $153&nbsp;million, $42&nbsp;million and $136&nbsp;million of the purchase price to FCC licenses, network
affiliations and goodwill, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><A
NAME="page_do1126_1_36"> </A> </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><B>Consolidation of Los Angeles Times' Production Operations  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In December&nbsp;2005, the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles Times</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> announced it would close its San Fernando Valley printing facility
in January&nbsp;2006 and consolidate production at its remaining three facilities in Los Angeles, Costa Mesa, and Irwindale, California. The closing of the printing facility resulted in the
elimination of approximately 120 positions from across the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles Times'</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> production facilities. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
a result of the facility closing, the Company reclassified the San Fernando Valley printing facility land and building as held for sale at Dec&nbsp;25, 2005. The Company recorded a
$2&nbsp;million pretax charge in the fourth quarter of 2005 to reduce the carrying value of the San Fernando Valley printing facility's land and building to $24&nbsp;million, the estimated fair
value of the assets less costs to sell the assets. The Company evaluated the machinery and equipment at the San Fernando Valley printing facility and determined that press and other related equipment
with a net book value of $16&nbsp;million will be abandoned. Therefore, the Company reduced its estimate of the useful life of the press and other related equipment and recorded accelerated
depreciation of $16&nbsp;million in the fourth quarter of 2005. The Company has idled the remaining San Fernando Valley machinery and equipment, which had a net book value of $34&nbsp;million at
Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005. The Company is currently evaluating alternative uses of this equipment. This evaluation is expected to be completed in 2006. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company recorded a pretax charge in the fourth quarter of 2005 of $22&nbsp;million, excluding severance related costs, as a result of its decision to close the San Fernando Valley
printing facility. A summary of the significant components of the $22&nbsp;million pretax charge is as follows (in&nbsp;millions): </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Employee Reductions  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company reduced its staff by approximately 900 positions in 2005 and recorded a pretax charge of $45&nbsp;million ($43&nbsp;million at publishing,
$1&nbsp;million at broadcasting&nbsp;and entertainment and $1&nbsp;million at corporate). The eliminations included 120 positions as a result of closing the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles
Times'</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> San Fernando Valley printing facility, as discussed above. As of Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, $7&nbsp;million had been paid and an accrual of $38&nbsp;million remained. The
Company recorded a pretax charge of $41&nbsp;million in 2004 related to the elimination of approximately 600 positions in its publishing segment. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>OTHER DEVELOPMENTS</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In February&nbsp;2004, a purported class action lawsuit was filed in New York Federal Court by certain advertisers of </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and
</FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, alleging that they were overcharged for advertising as a result of inflated
circulation numbers at these two publications. The purported class action also alleges that entities that paid a </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> subsidiary to deliver
advertising flyers were overcharged. In July&nbsp;2004, another lawsuit was filed in New York Federal Court by certain advertisers of </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> alleging
damages resulting from inflated </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> circulation numbers as well as federal and state antitrust violations. The Company intends to vigorously defend
these suits. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
June&nbsp;17, 2004, the Company publicly disclosed that it would reduce its reported circulation for both </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York for the 12-month period
ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2003 and the six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2004. The
circulation adjustments were the result of a review of reported circulation at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New
York, conducted by the Company's internal audit staff and the Audit Bureau of Circulations ("ABC"). Subsequent to the June&nbsp;17<SUP>th</SUP> disclosure, the Company continued its internal
review and found additional misstatements for these time periods, as well as misstatements that impacted the 12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2002. On Sept.&nbsp;10, 2004, the
Company announced additional revisions to the circulation figures for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the
12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2003 and the six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2004. In November&nbsp;2004, ABC released its audit reports for </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the 12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2003. In
March&nbsp;2005, ABC released its audit reports for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> for the six-month periods ending March&nbsp;31, 2004 and Sept.&nbsp;30,
2004. In May&nbsp;2005, ABC released its audit reports for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the six-month periods ending March&nbsp;31, 2004 and
Sept.&nbsp;30, 2004. Audited circulation figures for both </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday </I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for these periods
were within the ranges previously disclosed. After releasing these reports, ABC recalled </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday's</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> audit report and Publisher's Statements covering the
12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2002 and all of </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York's audit reports and Publisher's Statements covering the periods ending
March&nbsp;31, 2000 through Sept.&nbsp;30, 2002, stating that, due to insufficient information, they could not verify circulation for those periods. ABC also withdrew its unqualified opinion as to
the material fairness of the circulation reported for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> for the 12-month periods ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2000 and Sept.&nbsp;30,
2001, again citing insufficient information necessary to confirm the unqualified opinions. ABC's circulation audit at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> for the
six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2005 was issued in October&nbsp;2005 with no significant adjustments. ABC's circulation audit at </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2005
was issued in January&nbsp;2006 with no significant adjustments.
Circulation audits at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the period ending </FONT></P>

<!-- ZEQ.=3,SEQ=41,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=298690,FOLIO='38',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]DO1126A.;14',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:00' -->
<A NAME="page_do1126_1_39"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>September&nbsp;2005
are ongoing. </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, converted to free distribution in January&nbsp;2006. Due to this change, </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York's circulation for the period ending
September&nbsp;2005 and going forward will be audited by the Certified Audit of Circulations. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
a result of the misstatements of reported circulation at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, the
Company recorded a pretax charge of $35&nbsp;million in the second quarter of 2004 as its estimate of the probable
cost to settle with advertisers based upon facts available at July&nbsp;30, 2004, the date of the Company's second quarter 2004 Form&nbsp;10-Q filing. Subsequent to that date, the
Company found additional circulation misstatements, which increased the cost to settle with advertisers. As a result, the Company recorded an additional pretax charge of $55&nbsp;million in the
third quarter of 2004 to increase the estimate of the probable cost to settle with </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New
York, advertisers to a total of $90&nbsp;million. The Company will continue to evaluate the adequacy of this charge on an ongoing basis (see Note&nbsp;3 to the Company's consolidated financial
statements in Item 8). </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
addition to the advertiser lawsuits, several class action and shareholder derivative suits have been filed against the Company and certain of its current and former directors and
officers as a result of the circulation misstatements at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York. The suits, which are
currently pending in Illinois Federal and State Courts, allege breaches of fiduciary duties and other managerial and director failings under Delaware law, the federal securities laws and ERISA. The
Company believes the complaints are without merit and intends to vigorously defend the suits. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Securities and Exchange Commission, the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York and the Nassau County District Attorney are conducting inquiries into the
circulation practices at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York. The Company is cooperating fully with these
inquiries. The Company cannot predict with certainty the outcome of these inquiries. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
June&nbsp;2, 2003, the FCC adopted new media ownership rules, including a new television/newspaper cross-ownership rule. The new rule would eliminate the cross-ownership prohibition
entirely in markets with nine or more television stations and permit combinations of one newspaper and one television station in markets having from four to eight television stations. Under this rule,
the Company would be permitted to retain its newspaper and television operations in each of the five markets where it owns both&#151;New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, South Florida and Hartford.
In September&nbsp;2003, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit stayed the effectiveness of the new media ownership rules pending the outcome of appeals by advocacy groups
challenging the new rules. In June&nbsp;2004, the Third Circuit remanded the new rules to the FCC for further proceedings while keeping the stay in effect. On Jan.&nbsp;28, 2005, the Company and
other media companies filed a joint petition seeking United States Supreme Court review of the June&nbsp;2004 Third Circuit remand. On June&nbsp;13, 2005, the Supreme Court declined to review the
petition, without addressing the Constitutional arguments raised and without foreclosing additional appeals if the Company's interests are not adequately addressed as part of the FCC's remand
proceeding. While the Company remains optimistic that the cross-ownership ban will ultimately be loosened in major markets, it cannot predict with certainty the outcome of the FCC's remand proceeding.
See Item&nbsp;3, "Legal Proceedings" for a discussion of pending FCC rule review. </FONT></P>

expenses increased $13&nbsp;million in 2005 primarily due to increases in newsprint and ink and outside services expenses, partially offset by lower circulation distribution expense. Publishing
advertising revenues increased $16&nbsp;million in 2005, while publishing circulation revenues declined 7%, or $48&nbsp;million. Broadcasting and entertainment operating profit decreased 20%, or

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Cost of sales increased 1%, or $29&nbsp;million, in 2005 primarily due to higher newsprint and ink, programming and outside services expenses,
partially offset by a decline in circulation distribution expense. Compensation expense was flat compared with 2004. Newsprint and ink expense was up 3%, or $14&nbsp;million, in 2005, due to a
16%&nbsp;increase in newsprint costs per ton, partially offset by an 11%&nbsp;drop in consumption. The Company's newspapers are transitioning to lighter weight newsprint that on a per ton basis
costs more but yields more pages. The increase in newsprint cost per ton reflects increased market prices and the higher cost of lighter weight paper. Programming expenses increased 1%, or
$6&nbsp;million, in 2005 due to more program additions in 2005 compared to 2004. Outside services expense increased 11%, or $18&nbsp;million, in 2005 due largely to higher legal fees and outside
printing costs. Circulation distribution expense declined 1%, or $5&nbsp;million, primarily due to lower payments to outside contractors as a result of circulation volume declines. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Cost
of sales increased 3%, or $72&nbsp;million, in 2004. On a comparable basis, cost of sales was up 3%, or $66&nbsp;million, primarily due to higher compensation and newsprint and
ink expense, partially offset by a decline in programming expenses. Compensation expense rose 8%, or $77&nbsp;million, in 2004 due to higher retirement plan and other benefit expenses. On a
comparable basis, compensation expense increased 8%, or $76&nbsp;million, in 2004. Newsprint and ink expense rose 8%, or $35&nbsp;million, in 2004 as average newsprint cost per ton was up 12%,
while consumption declined 3% in 2004. Programming expenses decreased 6%, or $25&nbsp;million, in 2004 due to a decline in broadcast rights amortization expense related to fewer program additions in
2004 compared to 2003. On a comparable basis, programming expenses declined 7%, or $30&nbsp;million, in 2004. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Selling,
general and administrative ("SG&amp;A") expenses were down 6%, or $99&nbsp;million, in 2005. Compensation expense decreased 1%, or $5&nbsp;million, in 2005. Compensation expense
in 2005 included a severance charge of $45&nbsp;million for the elimination of approximately 900 positions and a pension curtailment gain of $18&nbsp;million, while 2004 compensation expense
included a severance charge of $41&nbsp;million for the elimination of about 600 positions in the publishing segment. Circulation expense decreased 6%, or $7&nbsp;million, in 2005. Other SG&amp;A
expenses declined $81&nbsp;million in 2005. Other SG&amp;A expenses in 2004 included a charge of $90&nbsp;million related to the anticipated settlement with advertisers regarding misstated circulation
at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Publishing  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Operating Revenues and Profit&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In 2005, publishing contributed 73% of the Company's revenues and 66% of its operating profits. Daily
newspaper revenue is derived principally from advertising and circulation sales, which accounted for 79% and 15%, respectively, of the publishing segment's total revenues in 2005. Advertising revenue
is comprised of three basic categories: retail, national and classified. Newspaper advertising volume is categorized as full run inches, part run inches or preprint pieces. Circulation revenue results
from the sale of newspapers. Other publications/services revenue accounted for 6% of the segment's total revenues in 2005 and includes syndication of editorial products, advertising placement
services, direct mail operations, cable television news programming, distribution of entertainment listings and other publishing-related activities. </FONT></P>

of certain advertising types used in this discussion are as follows: </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><A
NAME="page_dq1126_1_44"> </A> </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Publishing operating revenues in 2005 decreased 1% to $4.10&nbsp;billion, down from $4.13&nbsp;billion in 2004, due mainly to lower circulation revenue in Los Angeles, Chicago and
New York. In 2004, publishing operating revenues were up 2%, or $93&nbsp;million, compared with 2003, primarily due to increases in advertising revenue in Chicago, New York, Hartford, Los Angeles
and for the Spanish language newspaper, </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Operating
profit increased 5%, or $34&nbsp;million, in 2005 primarily due to lower one-time charges as described below. Operating profit decreased 18%, or
$159&nbsp;million, in 2004 primarily due to the charges described in the following paragraph, higher retirement plan and other benefit expenses, an increase in newsprint and ink expense and the
impact of new publications. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For
2005, publishing operating profit included a pretax charge of $22&nbsp;million for the shutdown of the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles Times'</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> San
Fernando Valley printing facility, $43&nbsp;million of severance charges for the elimination of over 800 positions and a pension curtailment gain of $13&nbsp;million, as a result of changes to the
retirement programs at the Company. For 2004, publishing operating profit included a pretax charge of $90&nbsp;million related to the anticipated settlement with advertisers regarding misstated
circulation at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the periods of September&nbsp;2001 through
March&nbsp;2004. Operating profit for 2004 also included a pretax charge of $41&nbsp;million for the elimination of about 600 positions. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Operating Revenues&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Total operating revenues decreased 1% in 2005 compared to 2004 and increased 2% in 2004 compared to 2003. Total

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Advertising Revenue and Volume&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Total advertising revenues were essentially flat in 2005 compared to 2004. Retail advertising revenue was
down 1%, or $7&nbsp;million, for the year as decreases in department stores, food&nbsp;&amp; drug stores, electronics and furniture/home furnishings categories, were partially offset by increases in
hardware/home improvement and other retail categories. Preprint revenues, which are primarily included in retail advertising, rose 2%, or $15&nbsp;million, due to increases at Los Angeles and
Chicago, partially offset by a decrease at Newsday. National advertising revenue
decreased 4%, or $29&nbsp;million, in 2005 as decreases in wireless, transportation, technology and movies categories were offset by an increase in the financial category. Classified advertising
revenues increased 5%, or $51&nbsp;million, in 2005 due to increases in real estate and help wanted of 15% and 13%, respectively, partially offset by an 8% decrease in auto. Interactive revenues,
which are included in the above categories, increased 43%, or $53&nbsp;million, in 2005. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Total
advertising revenues increased 4% in 2004 compared to 2003. Retail advertising revenue was up 2%, or $29&nbsp;million, for the year as increases in specialty merchandise,
furniture/home furnishings, food&nbsp;&amp; drug stores, hardware/home improvement and health care were partially offset by a decline in general merchandise and department stores. Preprint revenues,
which were the primary contributor to retail advertising growth, rose 9%, or $52&nbsp;million. Preprint revenue in Los Angeles and Chicago was up 19% and 8%, respectively. National advertising
revenue increased 4%, or $29&nbsp;million, in 2004 as </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Full run advertising inches were down 3% in 2005 due to decreases in all three major advertising categories. Full run retail advertising inches were down 4%
mainly due to decreases at Southern Connecticut and Baltimore, partially offset by increases at Orlando and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>. Full run national advertising inches
were down 6% in 2005 primarily due to decreases at Los Angeles, Orlando, Hartford and Baltimore. Full run classified advertising inches fell 2% for the year due to declines at South Florida,
Baltimore, </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and Los Angeles, partially offset by an increase at Orlando. Part run advertising inches were down 2% in 2005 due to a decrease at Los
Angeles, partially offset by an improvement at Newsday. Preprint advertising pieces rose 2% for the year due to increases at Los Angeles and Chicago, partially offset by a decrease at Newsday. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Full
run advertising inches were up 2% in 2004 primarily due to increases in retail and national advertising inches. Full run retail advertising inches were up 5% mainly due to increases
related to the new Chicago and Los Angeles editions of </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>. Full run national advertising inches were up 5% in 2004 primarily due to increases related
to </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>. Full run classified advertising inches fell 1% for the year due to declines at South Florida, Los Angeles and Orlando, partially offset by
increases related to </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>. Part
run advertising inches were up 6% in 2004 due to increases at Chicago and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>. Preprint advertising pieces rose 9% for the year due to increases at
Chicago, Los Angeles, </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and South Florida. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Circulation Revenues&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Circulation revenues were down 7% in 2005, primarily due to volume declines, as well as selectively higher discounting.
The largest revenue declines were at Los Angeles, Chicago and Newsday. Circulation revenues were down 3% in 2004, primarily due to declines at Los Angeles and Newsday. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Other Revenues&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Other revenues are derived from advertising placement services; the syndication of columns, features, information and comics
to newspapers; commercial printing operations; delivery of other publications; direct mail operations; cable television news programming; distribution of entertainment listings; and other
publishing-related activities. Other revenues were flat in 2005 compared to 2004. Other revenues decreased 2%, or $6&nbsp;million, in 2004 mainly due to decreases at New York and Orlando. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Publishing operating expenses decreased 2%, or $67&nbsp;million, in 2005 primarily due to the absence of the </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York charge and a decrease in compensation and circulation distribution expenses,
partially offset by increases in newsprint and ink, outside services and depreciation and amortization expense. Publishing operating expenses in 2004 included a charge of $90&nbsp;million related to
the anticipated settlement with advertisers regarding misstated circulation at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New
York. Compensation expense decreased 1%, or $14&nbsp;million, in 2005, primarily due to the $13&nbsp;million pension curtailment gain. The Company recorded $43&nbsp;million of severance charges
for the elimination of over 800 positions in 2005 and $41&nbsp;million of severance charges in for the elimination of about 600 positions in 2004. Circulation distribution expense declined 2%, or
$12&nbsp;million, due to lower payments to outside contractors primarily as a result of circulation volume declines. Newsprint and ink expense was up 3%, or $14&nbsp;million, in 2005, as newsprint
cost per ton increased 16%, while consumption decreased 11%. The Company's newspapers are transitioning to lighter weight newsprint that on a per ton basis costs more but yields more pages. The
increase in newsprint cost per ton reflects increased market prices and the higher cost of lighter weight paper. Outside services expense rose 7%, or $21&nbsp;million, in 2005 due largely to higher
legal fees and outside printing costs. Depreciation and amortization expense increased 7%, or $12&nbsp;million, primarily due to $16&nbsp;million of accelerated depreciation as a result of the
decision to shutdown the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles Times'</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> San Fernando Valley printing facility. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Publishing
operating expenses rose 8%, or $252&nbsp;million, in 2004 primarily due to higher compensation expense, increased newsprint and ink expense and the </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT
SIZE=2>, New York, charge, as well as an increase in expenses related to new publications.
Compensation expense rose 7%, or $95&nbsp;million, in 2004 primarily due to higher retirement plan and other benefit expenses and the $41&nbsp;million charge related to the elimination of
approximately 600 positions. Newsprint and ink expense was up 8%, or $36&nbsp;million, in 2004, as average newsprint prices increased 12%, while consumption decreased 3%. The Company recorded a
$90&nbsp;million charge for the estimated cost to settle with advertisers as a result of the reduced reported circulation at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York. The
increase in operating expenses associated with new publications, included in the above categories, totaled about $32&nbsp;million
in 2004. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Broadcasting and entertainment revenues decreased 6%, or $97&nbsp;million, in 2005 due mainly to lower television revenues, partially offset by an increase in
radio/entertainment revenues. Television revenues decreased 8%, or $103&nbsp;million, in 2005 due to lower advertising revenues. Television advertising revenues reflected weakness in the telecom,
automotive, and food categories, partially offset by increases in the financial and education categories. In addition, station revenues in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Boston were impacted by
lower audience ratings due in part to the use of Nielsen's Local People Meters ("LPMs") in these markets. Compared to Nielsen's previous measurement methodology, LPMs have tended to reduce the overall
share of broadcast television in relation to cable television and, within the broadcast television universe, disadvantage stations like Tribune's that target younger audiences. Radio/entertainment
revenues increased 2%, or $6&nbsp;million, in 2005 due to an increase at the Chicago Cubs, partially offset by lower revenues at Tribune Entertainment. Chicago Cubs revenues increased primarily as a
result of growth in marketing and broadcasting revenues, while Tribune Entertainment revenues declined due to lower syndication revenues. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Broadcasting
and entertainment revenues rose 2%, or $38&nbsp;million, in 2004 due mainly to increased television revenues. Excluding the acquisitions of KPLR-TV,
St.&nbsp;Louis (March&nbsp;2003), and KWBP-TV, Portland, Ore. (March&nbsp;2003) ("on a comparable basis"), broadcasting and entertainment revenues increased 2%, or
$24&nbsp;million. Television revenues increased 2%, or $30&nbsp;million, in 2004. Television advertising growth was driven by gains in the telecom, education and fast food/restaurant categories,
offset by softness in movies, retail and automobiles. On a comparable basis, television revenues were up 1%, or $16&nbsp;million, due to higher advertising revenues. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Operating
profit for broadcasting and entertainment was down 20%, or $108&nbsp;million, in 2005. Television operating profit declined 23%, or $123&nbsp;million, in 2005 due to lower
operating revenues and increased compensation and programming expenses. Radio/entertainment operating profit increased 80%, or $15&nbsp;million, in 2005 due to higher revenues at the Chicago Cubs
and lower operating expenses primarily due to fewer programs in production at Tribune Entertainment. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Operating
profit for broadcasting and entertainment was up 3%, or $15&nbsp;million, in 2004 due to increased television operating profit. On a comparable basis, operating profit was up
2%, or </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Broadcasting
and entertainment operating expenses increased 2%, or $23&nbsp;million, in 2004. On a comparable basis, broadcasting and entertainment operating expenses were up 1%, or

to higher retirement plan and other benefit expenses. On a comparable basis, compensation costs rose 9%, or $33&nbsp;million. Other expenses were up 5%, or $10&nbsp;million, in 2004 due to higher
selling and administrative costs. On a comparable basis, other expenses increased 4%, or $7&nbsp;million. Programming expenses dropped 6%, or $25&nbsp;million, in 2004 due to a decline in
broadcast rights amortization expense related to fewer program additions in 2004 compared to 2003. On a comparable basis, programming expenses decreased 7%, or $30&nbsp;million. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest

in 2004 and $2.9&nbsp;billion in 2003. Excluding the PHONES, outstanding debt was $2.8&nbsp;billion at year-end 2005, $2.0&nbsp;billion at year-end 2004 and
$2.0&nbsp;billion at year-end 2003. Including the PHONES, outstanding debt was $3.3&nbsp;billion at year-end 2005, $2.6&nbsp;billion at year-end 2004 and
$2.6&nbsp;billion at year-end 2003. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>LIQUIDITY AND CAPITAL RESOURCES</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Cash flow generated from operations is the Company's primary source of liquidity. Net cash provided by operations was $659&nbsp;million in 2005, down from
$1.1&nbsp;billion in 2004. The decrease was mainly due to the payment of the federal portion of the Matthew Bender and Mosby tax liabilities. The Company expects to fund dividends, capital
expenditures and other operating requirements with net cash provided by operations. Funding required for share repurchases and acquisitions is financed by available cash flow from operations and, if
necessary, by the issuance of debt and proceeds from the issuance of stock related to stock option exercises. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At

The revolving credit agreements allow the Company to elect one-month to twelve-month LIBOR rates, based on the term of the borrowing. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the one-month

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The

Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the Company had $924&nbsp;million of commercial paper outstanding. On Sept.&nbsp;30, 2005, the Company paid $880&nbsp;million to the Internal Revenue Service ("IRS"),
representing the federal tax and interest owed on the Matthew Bender and Mosby transactions, and financed the payment through the issuance of commercial paper. The Company expects to make related
state tax and interest payments of approximately $125&nbsp;million by mid 2006 (see Note&nbsp;12 to the Company's consolidated financial statements in Item&nbsp;8). </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The

Services ("Moody's"), Fitch Ratings ("Fitch") and Dominion Bond Rating Service ("Dominion"), respectively. The Company's senior unsecured long-term debt is rated "A-" by S&amp;P,
"A3" by Moody's, "A-" by Fitch and "A (low)" by Dominion. In addition, S&amp;P and Moody's have "stable" outlooks on the Company while Fitch has a "negative" outlook. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company has for several years maintained active debt shelf registration statements for its medium-term note program and other financing needs. The $778&nbsp;million

in February&nbsp;2006. Proceeds from any future debt issuances under the new shelf would be used for general corporate purposes, including repayment of debt, capital expenditures, working capital,
financing of acquisitions and stock repurchase programs. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
notes issued by the Employee Stock Ownership Plan ("ESOP") matured on Dec.&nbsp;16, 2003 and were fully repaid. The notes were unconditionally guaranteed by the Company as to

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Capital Spending&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company spent $206&nbsp;million for capital expenditures during 2005 and $217&nbsp;million in 2004
(see Note&nbsp;17 to the Company's consolidated financial statements in Item&nbsp;8 for capital spending by business segment.) The Company classifies capital expenditures that are expected to
provide a rate of return on investment above an internally set minimum rate as growth expenditures. The Company spent $87&nbsp;million in 2005 and $119&nbsp;million in 2004 on growth expenditures,
primarily in publishing. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Major
capital projects that were in process during 2005 included the expansion of preprint inserting operations and color press capacities and the implementation of a new standard
advertising system. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Capital
spending for the expansion of preprint inserting capacity in Los Angeles, South Florida and Orlando totaled $6&nbsp;million in 2005. During 2004 and 2003, the Company spent
$7&nbsp;million and $12&nbsp;million, respectively. The Los Angeles and South Florida expansions were operational in 2004. As of Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the installation of additional equipment and
systems at Orlando was in progress. The Orlando expansion is scheduled to be completed by mid-2006 with additional capital spending of approximately $4&nbsp;million in 2006. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company's Los Angeles, Chicago and South Florida newspapers are increasing their color press capacities. The Los Angeles expansion was operational in 2005, while the Chicago and
South Florida expansions are scheduled to be completed in late 2006. Capital spending for the color </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Effects of Inflation&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Consumer Price Index, a widely used measure of the impact of changing prices, has increased only moderately in
recent years, up between 2% and 3% each year since 1991. This level of inflation has not impacted the Company's operations significantly, nor have historically higher inflation levels that prevailed
prior to 1991. The principal effect of inflation on the Company's operating results is to increase costs. Subject to normal competitive conditions, the Company generally has demonstrated an ability to
raise sales prices to offset these cost increases. </FONT></P>

shareholders' equity. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;During the last 12 quarters preceding Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, market price movements caused the fair value of the Company's common stock investments
in publicly traded companies to change by 10% or more in six of the quarters, by 20% or more in three of the quarters and by 30% or more in two of the quarters. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Derivatives and Related Trading Securities&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company issued 8&nbsp;million PHONES in April&nbsp;1999 indexed to the value of its
investment in 16&nbsp;million shares of Time Warner common stock (see Note&nbsp;8 to the Company's consolidated financial statements in Item&nbsp;8). Beginning in the second quarter of 1999,
this investment in Time Warner is classified as a trading security, and changes in its fair value, net of the changes in the fair value of the related derivative component of the PHONES, are recorded
in the statement of income. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At
maturity, the PHONES will be redeemed at the greater of the then market value of two shares of Time Warner common stock or the principal value of the PHONES ($156.84 per PHONES at
Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005). At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, the PHONES carrying value was approximately $510&nbsp;million and $585&nbsp;million, respectively. Since the issuance of
the PHONES in April&nbsp;1999, changes in the fair value of the derivative component of the PHONES have partially offset changes in the fair value of the related Time Warner shares. There have been
and may continue to be periods with significant non-cash increases or decreases to the Company's net income pertaining to the PHONES and the related Time Warner shares. </FONT></P>

<A NAME="page_fb1126_1_59"> </A>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2><B>REPORT OF INDEPENDENT REGISTERED PUBLIC ACCOUNTING FIRM  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>To
the Board of Directors and Shareholders of Tribune Company: </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We
have completed integrated audits of Tribune Company's 2005 and 2004 consolidated financial statements and of its internal control over financial reporting as of December&nbsp;25,
2005, and an audit of its 2003 consolidated financial statements in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). Our opinions, based on our audits,
are presented below. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Consolidated financial statements and financial statement schedule  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements listed in the accompanying index present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of Tribune
Company and its subsidiaries at December&nbsp;25, 2005 and December&nbsp;26, 2004, and the results of their operations and their cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended
December&nbsp;25, 2005 in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. In addition, in our opinion, the financial statement schedule listed in the
accompanying index presents fairly, in all material respects, the information set forth therein when read in conjunction with the related consolidated financial statements. These financial statements
and financial statement schedule are the responsibility of the Company's management. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements and financial statement schedule based on
our audits. We conducted our audits of these statements in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). Those standards require that we plan and
perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free
of material misstatement. An audit of financial statements includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements, assessing the accounting
principles used and significant estimates made by management, and evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
discussed in Note&nbsp;1 to the consolidated financial statements, the Company changed the manner in which it evaluates certain indefinite-lived intangible assets for impairment. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Internal control over financial reporting  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Also, in our opinion, management's assessment, included in the accompanying Management's Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting, that the Company
maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of December&nbsp;25, 2005 based on criteria established in </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Internal Control&#151;Integrated
Framework</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO), is fairly stated, in all material respects, based on those criteria.
Furthermore, in our opinion, the Company maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of December&nbsp;25, 2005, based on criteria established in </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Internal Control&#151;Integrated
Framework</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> issued by the COSO. The Company's management is responsible for maintaining effective internal control
over financial reporting and for its assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting. Our responsibility is to express opinions on management's assessment and on the
effectiveness of the Company's internal control over financial reporting based on our audit. We conducted our audit of internal control over financial reporting in accordance with the standards of the
Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether effective internal control over
financial reporting was maintained in all material respects. An audit of internal control over financial reporting includes obtaining an understanding of internal control over financial reporting,
evaluating management's assessment, testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control, and performing such other procedures as we consider necessary in the
circumstances. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinions. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>59</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>
<!-- ZEQ.=2,SEQ=62,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=578746,FOLIO='59',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]FB1126A.;8',USER='ANEETZ',CD='24-FEB-2006;17:40' -->
<A NAME="page_fb1126_1_60"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A
company's internal control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of
financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company's internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures
that (i)&nbsp;pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (ii)&nbsp;provide
reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and
expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorizations of management and directors of the company; and (iii)&nbsp;provide
reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the company's assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Because
of its inherent limitations, internal control over financial reporting may not prevent or detect misstatements. Also, projections of any evaluation of effectiveness to future
periods are subject to the risk that controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>
<IMG SRC="g943694.jpg" ALT="SIGNATURE" WIDTH="262" HEIGHT="54">

LLP<BR>
Chicago, Illinois<BR>
February&nbsp;21, 2006 </FONT></P>

<A NAME="page_fb1126_1_61"> </A>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2><B>MANAGEMENT'S RESPONSIBILITY FOR FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND<BR>
MANAGEMENT'S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL REPORTING  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Management's Responsibility for Financial Statements  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Management is responsible for the preparation, integrity and fair presentation of the Company's consolidated financial statements and related financial
information included in this Annual Report on Form&nbsp;10-K to shareholders. The consolidated financial statements have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America and necessarily include certain amounts that are based on management's best estimates and judgments. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
system of internal control over financial reporting is periodically assessed for its effectiveness and is augmented by written policies and procedures, the careful selection and
training of qualified personnel and a program of internal audit. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
consolidated financial statements were audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, an independent registered public accounting firm, and their report is shown on pages&nbsp;59 and 60.
PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP was given unrestricted access to all financial records and related data, including minutes of all meetings of shareholders, the Board of Directors and committees of the
Board. The Company believes that all representations made to the independent accountants during their audits were valid and appropriate. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Audit Committee of the Board of Directors is responsible for reviewing and monitoring the Company's financial reporting and accounting practices. The Audit Committee consists of four
independent directors. The Committee meets with representatives of management, the independent registered public accounting firm and internal auditors to discuss financial reporting, accounting and
internal control matters. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP and the internal auditors have direct access to the Audit Committee. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Management's Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting, designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding
the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. As
of Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the Company's management conducted an evaluation of the effectiveness of the design and operation of the Company's internal control over financial reporting based on criteria
established in </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Internal Control&#151;Integrated Framework</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission and
concluded that the Company's internal control over financial reporting was effective as of that date. Our management's assessment of the effectiveness of the Company's internal control over financial
reporting as of Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 has been audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, an independent registered public accounting firm, as stated in their report which appears herein. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2><A
