<BR><FONT SIZE=2><B>TRIBUNE COMPANY AND SUBSIDIARIES  </B></FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2><B> NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>NOTE 1: SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The significant accounting policies of Tribune Company and subsidiaries (the "Company"), as summarized below, conform with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America and reflect practices appropriate to the Company's businesses. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Nature of Operations&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company is a media and entertainment company. Through its subsidiaries, the Company is engaged in newspaper
publishing, television and radio broadcasting and entertainment. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Fiscal Year&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company's fiscal year ends on the last Sunday in December. Fiscal years 2005, 2004 and 2003 each comprised 52&nbsp;weeks. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Principles of Consolidation&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Tribune Company and all majority-owned
subsidiaries. In general, investments comprising 20 to 50&nbsp;percent of the voting stock of companies and certain partnership interests are accounted for using the equity method. All other
investments are generally accounted for using the cost method. All significant intercompany transactions are eliminated. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company evaluates its investments and other transactions for consolidation under the provisions of Financial Accounting Standards Board ("FASB") Interpretation No.&nbsp;46,
"Consolidation of Variable Interest Entities" ("FIN&nbsp;46"), issued in January&nbsp;2003. The Company holds significant variable interests, as defined by FIN&nbsp;46, in CareerBuilder, LLC,
Classified Ventures, LLC, ShopLocal, LLC (formerly CrossMedia Services,&nbsp;Inc.) and Topix, LLC, but the Company has determined that it is not the primary beneficiary of these entities. The
Company's maximum loss exposure related to these entities is limited to its equity investments in CareerBuilder, LLC, Classified Ventures, LLC, ShopLocal, LLC (formerly
CrossMedia Services,&nbsp;Inc.) and Topix, LLC, which were $81&nbsp;million, $42&nbsp;million, $25&nbsp;million and $15&nbsp;million, respectively, at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005. At
Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, the Company's equity investments in CareerBuilder, LLC, Classified Ventures, LLC and ShopLocal, LLC (formerly CrossMedia Services,&nbsp;Inc.) were $81&nbsp;million,
$8&nbsp;million and $24&nbsp;million, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Presentation&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Certain prior year financial information has been reclassified to conform to the current year presentation. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Revenue Recognition&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company's primary sources of revenue are from the sales of advertising space in published issues of its newspapers
and on interactive websites owned by, or affiliated with, the Company; distribution of preprinted advertising inserts in its newspapers; sales of newspapers to distributors and individual subscribers;
and sales of airtime on its television and radio stations. Newspaper advertising revenue is recorded, net of agency commissions, when advertisements are published in newspapers. Website advertising
revenue is recognized ratably over the contract period or as services are delivered, as appropriate. Proceeds from subscriptions are deferred and are included in revenue on a pro-rata
basis over the term of the subscriptions. Broadcast revenue is recorded, net of agency commissions, when commercials are aired. The Company records rebates when earned as a reduction of advertising
revenue. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Use of Estimates&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The preparation of financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported in the financial statements and accompanying notes. Actual results could differ from these estimates. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>69</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>

<!-- ZEQ.=1,SEQ=72,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=736754,FOLIO='69',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]FK1126A.;15',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:00' -->
<A NAME="page_fk1126_1_70"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Cash and Cash Equivalents&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Cash and cash equivalents are stated at cost, which approximates market value. Investments with original
maturities of three months or less at the time of purchase are considered to be cash equivalents. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Accounts Receivable&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company's accounts receivable are primarily due from advertisers. Credit is extended based on an evaluation of each
customer's financial condition, and generally collateral is not required. The Company maintains an allowance for uncollectible accounts, rebates and volume discounts. This allowance is determined
based on historical write-off experience and any known specific collectibility exposures. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Inventories&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Inventories are stated at the lower of cost or market. Cost is determined on the last-in, first-out
("LIFO") basis for newsprint and on the first-in, first-out ("FIFO") basis for all other inventories. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Broadcast Rights&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Broadcast rights consist principally of rights to broadcast syndicated programs, sports and feature films and are stated at
the lower of cost or estimated net realizable value. The total cost of these rights is recorded as an asset and a liability when the program becomes available for broadcast. Syndicated program rights
that have limited showings are generally amortized using an accelerated method as programs are aired. Sports and feature film rights are amortized using the straight-line method. The
current portion of broadcast rights represents those rights available for broadcast that are expected to be amortized in the succeeding year. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company maintains an allowance for programming that is not expected to be aired by the end of the contract period. This allowance for excess programming inventory is based on a
program-by-program review of the Company's five-year broadcast plans and historical write-off trends. The total reserve balance at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005
and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004 was $4&nbsp;million and $5&nbsp;million, respectively. Actual write-offs in 2005 and 2004 were $1&nbsp;million and $12&nbsp;million, respectively. Future
write-offs can vary based on changes in consumer viewing trends and the availability and costs of other programming. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Properties&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Property, plant and equipment are stated at cost. The Company capitalizes major property, plant and equipment additions,
improvements and replacements, as well as interest incurred during construction of major facilities and equipment. Depreciation is computed using the straight-line method over the
following estimated useful lives: 10 to 40&nbsp;years for buildings, 7 to 20&nbsp;years for newspaper printing presses and 3 to 10&nbsp;years for all other equipment. Expenditures for repairs
and maintenance of existing assets are charged to expense as incurred. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Goodwill and other intangible assets are summarized in Note&nbsp;5. The Company periodically reviews
goodwill and certain intangible assets no longer being amortized for impairment in accordance with Financial Accounting Standard ("FAS") No.&nbsp;142, "Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets." Under
FAS No.&nbsp;142, the impairment review of goodwill and other intangible assets not subject to amortization must be based generally on fair values. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
estimated fair value of the reporting units to which goodwill is allocated is determined using multiples of operating cash flows for purposes of analyzing goodwill for impairment.
The estimated fair values of other assets subject to the annual impairment review, which include newspaper mastheads and FCC licenses, are calculated based on projected future discounted cash flow
analyses. The development of market multiples and cash flow projections used in the analyses requires the use of assumptions, including assumptions regarding revenue and market growth. The analyses
use discount rates based on specific economic factors in the publishing and broadcasting industries. These assumptions reflect the </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>70</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>
<!-- ZEQ.=2,SEQ=73,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=195935,FOLIO='70',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]FK1126A.;15',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:00' -->
<A NAME="page_fk1126_1_71"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>Company's
best estimates, but these items involve inherent uncertainties based on market conditions generally outside of the Company's control. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
the fourth quarter of 2004, the Company elected to early adopt the provisions of the FASB's Emerging Issues Task Force Topic No.&nbsp;D-108, which requires the use of a
direct valuation method for valuing intangible assets, such as FCC licenses, and reviewing them for impairment. Historically, the Company had been using a residual valuation method to review its FCC
licenses for impairment each year. A direct valuation method generally results in a lower valuation than does a residual valuation method. The Company performed an impairment review of its FCC
licenses for the years ended Dec.&nbsp;28, 2003 using a residual method. No impairments were required as a result of the analyses performed in 2003. The effect of changing to a direct valuation
method for the 2004 FCC licenses impairment review was a pretax charge of $29&nbsp;million ($18&nbsp;million after-tax). The charge was recorded in the fourth quarter of 2004 as a
cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle in the consolidated statements of income. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Upon
the adoption of FAS No.&nbsp;142 at the beginning of fiscal 2002, the Company treated the intangible assets associated with network affiliation agreements as having indefinite
lives and stopped recording amortization expense on these assets. In December&nbsp;2003, the staff of the Securities and Exchange Commission provided guidance regarding their accounting position in
this area indicating that network affiliation agreements should be amortized. As a result, the Company began amortizing these assets in the fourth quarter of 2003 using a 40-year life. The
Company believes the 40-year life is representative of the remaining expected useful life of the network affiliation intangibles. The provisions of FAS No.&nbsp;142 required the Company
to perform an impairment analysis at the time of a change in the estimated useful life of an intangible asset which was previously not being amortized. No adjustment to the network affiliation
intangible assets was required as a result of this impairment review performed in the fourth quarter of 2003. Beginning in 2004, the Company no longer performs an annual test of the impairment of its
network affiliation agreements under FAS No.&nbsp;142, but will perform an impairment test if indicators of impairment are present, as required by FAS No.&nbsp;144, "Accounting for the Impairment
or Disposal of Long-Lived Assets." </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Investments&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company records its investments in debt and equity securities at fair value, except for debt securities that the Company
intends to hold to maturity and equity securities that are accounted for under the equity method or that are issued by private companies. Except for 16&nbsp;million Time Warner shares (see
"Derivative Instruments" below), investments are currently classified as available-for-sale, and accordingly, the difference between cost and fair value, net of related tax
effects, is recorded in the accumulated other comprehensive income component of shareholders' equity. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Derivative Instruments&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>FAS No.&nbsp;133, "Accounting for Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities," requires all derivative
instruments to be recorded in the balance sheet at fair value. Changes in the fair value of derivative instruments are recognized periodically in income. The provisions of FAS No.&nbsp;133 affect
the Company's accounting for its 8&nbsp;million Exchangeable Subordinated Debentures due 2029 ("PHONES") (see Note&nbsp;8) and its interest rate swap related to its $100&nbsp;million 7.5%
debentures (see Note&nbsp;8). </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under
the provisions of FAS No.&nbsp;133, the initial value of the PHONES was split into a debt component and a derivative component. Changes in the fair value of the derivative
component of the PHONES are recorded in the statement of income. Beginning in the second quarter of 1999, changes in the fair value of the related 16&nbsp;million Time Warner shares are also
recorded in the statement of income and should at least partially offset changes in the fair value of the derivative component of the PHONES. However, there have been, and may continue to be, periods
with significant non-cash </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>71</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>
<!-- ZEQ.=3,SEQ=74,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=504876,FOLIO='71',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]FK1126A.;15',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:00' -->
<A NAME="page_fk1126_1_72"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>increases
or decreases to the Company's net income pertaining to the PHONES and the related Time Warner shares. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
carrying values of the Company's derivative instruments approximate fair value. The fair values of the PHONES were determined by reference to market values resulting from trading on
a national securities exchange. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company's interest rate swap is a fair value hedge and is used to manage exposure to market risk associated with changes in interest rates. The changes in fair value of the swap
agreement and the related debt instrument are recorded in income. Changes in the fair value of the swap agreement offset changes in the fair value of the related debt (see Note&nbsp;8). </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Pension Plans&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Retirement benefits are provided to employees through pension plans sponsored either by the Company or by unions. Under the
Company-sponsored plans, pension benefits are primarily a function of both the years of service and the level of compensation for a specified number of years, depending on the plan. It is the
Company's policy to fund the minimum for Company-sponsored pension plans as required by ERISA. Contributions made to union-sponsored plans are based upon collective bargaining agreements. Additional
information is provided in Note&nbsp;13. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Postretirement Benefits Other than Pensions&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company provides certain health care and life insurance benefits for retired employees. The
expected cost of providing these benefits is accrued over the years that the employees render services. It is the Company's policy to fund postretirement benefits as claims are incurred. Additional
information is provided in Note&nbsp;13. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Self-Insurance&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company self-insures for certain employee medical and disability income benefits, workers'
compensation costs and automobile and general liability claims. The recorded liabilities for self-insured risks are calculated using actuarial methods and are not discounted. The recorded
liabilities for self-insured risks totaled $113&nbsp;million and $106&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Deferred Income&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Deferred income arises in the normal course of business from advance subscription payments for newspapers, interactive
advertising sales and prepaid ticket revenue related to the Chicago Cubs. Deferred income is recognized in the period it is earned. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Stock-Based Compensation&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company accounts for its stock-based compensation plans in accordance with Accounting Principles Board ("APB")
Opinion No.&nbsp;25 and related interpretations. Under APB&nbsp;No.&nbsp;25, no compensation expense is recorded because the exercise price of employee stock options equals the market price of
the underlying stock on the date of grant. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
June&nbsp;24, 2005, the Company accelerated the vesting of certain stock options granted on Feb.&nbsp;11, 2003 and Feb.&nbsp;10, 2004, totaling 2.4&nbsp;million in each year.
Unvested stock options awarded to the then current executive officers of the Company on these grant dates, which aggregated 0.8&nbsp;million and 0.6&nbsp;million, respectively, were not
accelerated at that time. On Dec.&nbsp;16, 2005, the Company accelerated the vesting of all stock options granted on Feb.&nbsp;8, 2005, totaling 3.5&nbsp;million. Also on Dec.&nbsp;16, 2005,
the Company accelerated the remaining unvested stock options granted to the then current executive officers of the Company on Feb.&nbsp;11, 2003 and Feb.&nbsp;10, 2004, totaling 0.4&nbsp;million
in both years. All other terms and conditions of the stock option grants remain unchanged. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
accordance with APB No.&nbsp;25 and related interpretations, the acceleration of vesting of these stock options did not require accounting recognition in the Company's income
statement. The exercise prices of the 2003, 2004 and 2005 grants were $45.90, $52.05 and $40.59, respectively, and the </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>72</FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>Company's

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
accelerated vesting of these stock options was one of several actions the Company has recently taken to reduce stock-based compensation expense that will be recorded in future years
with the adoption of Financial Accounting Standard ("FAS") No.&nbsp;123R (see "New Accounting Standards" discussion below). Over the last two years, the Company has reduced the number of stock
options granted by approximately 45%. Also, beginning in 2004, option grants have 8-year terms, down from 10&nbsp;years for grants in previous years, and do not have a replacement option feature. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under

of the award and is recognized as compensation expense over the vesting period. Had compensation cost for the Company's stock-based compensation plans been determined consistent with FAS
No.&nbsp;123, the Company's full year net income and EPS would have been reduced to the following pro forma amounts (in thousands, except per share data): </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Income Taxes&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Provisions for federal and state income taxes are calculated on reported pretax earnings based on current tax laws and also
include, in the current period, the cumulative effect of any changes in tax rates from those used previously in determining deferred tax assets and liabilities. Taxable income reported to the taxing
jurisdictions in which the Company operates often differs from pretax earnings because some items of income and expense are recognized in different time periods for income tax purposes. The Company
provides deferred taxes on these temporary differences in accordance with FAS No.&nbsp;109, "Accounting for Income Taxes." Taxable income also may differ from pretax earnings due to statutory
provisions under which specific revenues are exempt from taxation and specific expenses are not allowable as deductions. The Company establishes reserves for income tax when it is probable that one or
more of the taxing authorities will challenge and disallow a position taken by the Company in its income tax returns and the resulting liability is estimable. The consolidated tax provision and
related accruals include estimates of the potential taxes and related interest as deemed appropriate. These estimates are reevaluated and adjusted, if appropriate, on a quarterly basis. Although
management believes its estimates and judgments are reasonable, the
resolutions of the Company's tax issues are unpredictable and could result in tax liabilities that are significantly higher or lower than that which has been provided by the Company. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Comprehensive Income&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Comprehensive income consists of net income and other gains and losses affecting shareholders' equity that, under
accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, are excluded from net income. Other comprehensive income (loss) primarily includes gains and losses on marketable securities
classified as available-for-sale and changes in minimum pension liabilities. The Company's comprehensive income (loss) is summarized in Note&nbsp;16. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>New Accounting Standards&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In December&nbsp;2004, the FASB issued FAS No.&nbsp;123R, "Share-Based Payment." FAS No.&nbsp;123R supercedes
APB No.&nbsp;25, FAS No.&nbsp;123, as amended by FAS No.&nbsp;148, and related interpretations. Under FAS No.&nbsp;123R, compensation cost is measured at the grant date based on the estimated
fair value of the award and is required to be recognized as compensation expense over the vesting period. The Company plans to adopt FAS No.&nbsp;123R in the first quarter of 2006 using the modified
prospective application, which requires the recognition of share-based compensation costs as if the provisions of the standard had been in effect since Dec.&nbsp;25, 1994 (the beginning of the
Company's 1995 fiscal year). The Company expects to record approximately $33&nbsp;million of pretax compensation expense in 2006 related to equity grants in 2006 and prior years, as well as the
Company's ESPP. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Earnings Per Share ("EPS")&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Basic EPS is computed by dividing net income attributable to common shares by the weighted average number of
common shares outstanding during the period. Diluted EPS </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>74</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>
<!-- ZEQ.=6,SEQ=77,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=16664,FOLIO='74',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]FK1126A.;15',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:00' -->
<A NAME="page_fk1126_1_75"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>for
the year ended Dec.&nbsp;28, 2003 was computed assuming that the Series&nbsp;B convertible preferred shares held by the Company's Employee Stock Ownership Plan ("ESOP") and the Liquid Yield
Option Notes ("LYONs") debt securities had been converted into common shares as of the beginning of fiscal year 2003. The Series&nbsp;B convertible preferred shares were converted into approximately
15.4&nbsp;million shares of common stock on Dec.&nbsp;16, 2003, and the LYONs were converted into approximately 7.0&nbsp;million shares of common stock during June&nbsp;2003. Therefore,
weighted average converted shares for the Series&nbsp;B preferred stock and LYONs were used in the 2003 calculation. In addition, weighted average common shares outstanding were adjusted for the
dilutive effect of stock options. The Company's stock options and convertible securities are included in the calculation of diluted EPS only when their effects are dilutive. In the 2005, 2004 and 2003
calculations of diluted EPS, 2.9&nbsp;million, 2.3&nbsp;million and 2.3&nbsp;million shares, respectively, of the Company's Series&nbsp;C, D-1 and D-2 convertible
preferred stocks, and 35.5&nbsp;million, 10.6&nbsp;million and 3.2&nbsp;million shares, respectively, of the Company's outstanding options, were not reflected because their effects were
antidilutive. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>NOTE 2: CHANGES IN OPERATIONS AND NON-OPERATING ITEMS</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Acquisitions&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company had no significant acquisitions in 2005 and 2004. The Company completed acquisitions totaling approximately
$275&nbsp;million in 2003 for cash and other consideration, including the value of the Denver radio station group assets that were divested in an exchange transaction during 2003. The results of the
acquired companies are included in the consolidated statements of income since their respective dates of acquisition. None of these acquisitions were material in relation to the Company's consolidated
financial statements. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
March&nbsp;21, 2003, the Company acquired the stock of KPLR-TV, St.&nbsp;Louis, and the assets of KWBP-TV, Portland, Ore., from ACME Communications for a
total of $275&nbsp;million. The Company acquired the stock of KPLR-TV for $200&nbsp;million in cash. The acquisition of the assets of KWBP-TV was structured as a
like-kind asset exchange for income tax purposes. It was funded with the remaining assets of the Denver radio station group (KKHK-FM, now known as KQMT-FM) with an
estimated fair market value of $55&nbsp;million, plus $20&nbsp;million in cash. The Company allocated $153&nbsp;million, $42&nbsp;million and $136&nbsp;million of the purchase price to FCC
licenses, network affiliations and goodwill, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Consolidation of Los Angeles Times' Production Operations  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In December&nbsp;2005, the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles Times</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> announced it would close its San Fernando Valley printing facility
in January&nbsp;2006 and consolidate production at its remaining three facilities in Los Angeles, Costa Mesa, and Irwindale, California. The closing of the printing facility resulted in the
elimination of approximately 120 positions from across the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles Times'</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> production facilities. </FONT></P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE=2>77</FONT></P>

<HR NOSHADE>
<P style='page-break-before:always'></p>
<!-- ZEQ.=1,SEQ=80,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=461181,FOLIO='77',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]FM1126A.;14',USER='JMAHER',CD='25-FEB-2006;22:33' -->
<A NAME="page_fm1126_1_78"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
a result of the facility closing, the Company reclassified the San Fernando Valley printing facility land and building as held for sale at Dec&nbsp;25, 2005. The Company recorded a
$2&nbsp;million pretax charge in the fourth quarter of 2005 to reduce the carrying value of the San Fernando Valley printing facility's land and building to $24&nbsp;million, the estimated fair
value of the assets less costs to sell the assets. The Company evaluated the machinery and equipment at the San Fernando Valley printing facility and determined that press and other related equipment
with a net book value of $16&nbsp;million will be abandoned. Therefore, the Company reduced its estimate of the useful life of the press and other related equipment and recorded accelerated
depreciation of $16&nbsp;million in the fourth quarter of 2005. The Company has idled the remaining San Fernando Valley machinery and equipment, which had a net
book value of $34&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005. The Company is currently evaluating alternative uses of this equipment. This evaluation is expected to be completed in 2006. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company recorded a pretax charge in the fourth quarter of 2005 of $22&nbsp;million, excluding severance related costs, as a result of its decision to close the San Fernando Valley
printing facility. A summary of the significant components of the $22&nbsp;million pretax charge is as follows (in thousands): </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Employee Reductions  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company reduced its staff by approximately 900 positions in 2005 and recorded a pretax charge of $45&nbsp;million ($43&nbsp;million at publishing,
$1&nbsp;million at broadcasting&nbsp;&amp; entertainment and $1&nbsp;million at corporate). The eliminations included 120 positions as a result of closing the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles
Times'</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> San Fernando Valley printing facility, as discussed above. As of Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, $7&nbsp;million had been paid and an accrual of $38&nbsp;million remained. The
Company recorded a pretax charge of $41&nbsp;million in 2004 related to the elimination of approximately 600 positions in its publishing segment. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In February&nbsp;2004, a purported class action lawsuit was filed in New York Federal Court by certain advertisers of </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;and
</FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, alleging that they were overcharged for advertising as a result of
inflated circulation numbers at these two publications. The purported class action also alleges that entities that paid a </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> subsidiary to deliver
advertising flyers were overcharged. In July&nbsp;2004, another lawsuit was filed in New York Federal Court by certain advertisers of </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday </I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>alleging
damages resulting from inflated </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> circulation numbers as well as federal and state antitrust violations. The Company intends to vigorously defend
these suits. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
June&nbsp;17, 2004, the Company publicly disclosed that it would reduce its reported circulation for both </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York for the 12-month period
ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2003 and the six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2004. The
circulation adjustments were the result of a review of reported circulation at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New
York, conducted by the Company's internal audit staff and the Audit Bureau of Circulations ("ABC"). Subsequent to the June&nbsp;17<SUP>th</SUP> disclosure, the Company continued its internal
review and found additional misstatements for these time periods, as well as misstatements that impacted the 12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2002. On Sept.&nbsp;10, 2004, the
Company announced additional revisions to the circulation figures for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the
12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2003 and the six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2004. In November&nbsp;2004, ABC released its audit reports for </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the 12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2003. In
March&nbsp;2005, ABC released its audit reports for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> for the six-month periods ending March&nbsp;31, 2004 and Sept.&nbsp;30,
2004. In May&nbsp;2005, ABC released its audit reports for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the six-month periods ending March&nbsp;31, 2004 and
Sept.&nbsp;30, 2004. Audited circulation figures for both </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday </I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for these periods
were within the ranges previously disclosed. After releasing these reports, ABC recalled </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday's</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> audit report and Publisher's Statements covering the
12-month period ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2002 and all of </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York's audit reports and Publisher's Statements covering the periods ending
March&nbsp;31, 2000 through Sept.&nbsp;30, 2002, stating that, due to insufficient information, they could not verify circulation for those periods. ABC also withdrew its unqualified opinion as to
the material fairness of the circulation reported for </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> for the 12-month periods ending Sept.&nbsp;30, 2000 and Sept.&nbsp;30,
2001, again citing insufficient information necessary to confirm the unqualified opinions. ABC's circulation audit at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> for the
six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2005 was issued in October&nbsp;2005 with no significant adjustments. ABC's circulation audit at </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, for the six-month period ending March&nbsp;31, 2005
was issued in January&nbsp;2006 with no </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
a result of the misstatements of reported circulation at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, the

the date of the Company's second quarter 2004 Form&nbsp;10-Q filing. Subsequent to that date, the Company found additional circulation misstatements, which increased the cost to settle
with advertisers. As a result, the Company recorded an additional pretax charge of $55&nbsp;million in the third quarter of 2004 to increase the estimate of the probable cost to settle with </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and
</FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York, advertisers to a total of $90&nbsp;million. The Company will continue to
evaluate the adequacy of this charge on an ongoing basis. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition to the advertiser lawsuits, several class action and shareholder derivative suits have been filed against the Company and certain of
its current and former directors and officers as a result of the circulation misstatements at </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Hoy</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, New York. The suits, which are currently
pending in Illinois Federal and State Courts, allege breaches of fiduciary duties and other managerial and
director failings under Delaware law, the federal securities laws and ERISA. The Company believes the complaints are without merit and intends to vigorously defend the suits. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The

inquiries. The Company cannot predict with certainty the outcome of these inquiries. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>NOTE 6: TMCT&nbsp;I AND TMCT&nbsp;II</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In connection with the Company's acquisition of Times Mirror in 2000, the Company acquired investments in TMCT&nbsp;I and TMCT&nbsp;II. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>TMCT I&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In 1997, Times Mirror completed a transaction involving agreements with its largest shareholders, Chandler Trust
No.&nbsp;1 and Chandler Trust No.&nbsp;2 (collectively, the "Chandler Trusts") which resulted in the formation of a new limited liability company, TMCT, LLC ("TMCT&nbsp;I"). As a result of the
Company's acquisition of Times Mirror, the Chandler Trusts became significant shareholders of the Company. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At
Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the assets of TMCT&nbsp;I included 13&nbsp;million shares of the Company's common stock and 442,596 shares of the Company's Series&nbsp;C preferred stock
(collectively, "TMCT&nbsp;I Shares"); eight real properties ("Real Properties") and a portfolio of fixed income and equity investments ("TMCT&nbsp;I Portfolio"). TMCT&nbsp;I has no outstanding
debt. The estimated fair market value of the TMCT&nbsp;I assets at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004 is shown in the table below (in thousands): </FONT></P>

<!-- User-specified TAGGED TABLE -->
<TABLE WIDTH="100%" BORDER=0 CELLSPACING=0 CELLPADDING=0>
<TR VALIGN="BOTTOM">

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company leases the Real Properties from TMCT&nbsp;I and accounts for the lease as a property financing obligation in its consolidated balance sheet. On
Aug.&nbsp;8, 2009, the end of the lease term, the Company has the option to purchase all of the Real Properties for their fair market value. If the Real Properties are not purchased by the Company,
they will remain the assets of TMCT&nbsp;I and may, as provided for under the terms of the lease agreement, be leased by the Company at fair market value
rent. The agreement provides for two additional 12-year lease terms with fair market value purchase options at the end of each term. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company and the Chandler Trusts share in the cash flows of the various assets held by TMCT&nbsp;I. The cash flows from the Real Properties and the TMCT&nbsp;I Portfolio are
largely allocated to the Chandler Trusts, while the cash flows from the TMCT&nbsp;I Shares are largely allocated to the </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company's investment in TMCT&nbsp;I totaled $83&nbsp;million, $82&nbsp;million and $99&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004 and Dec.&nbsp;28, 2003,
respectively. In 2005, 2004 and 2003, the Company recognized equity income of $2&nbsp;million in each year related to the TMCT&nbsp;I Portfolio. During 2005, 2004 and 2003, the Company recorded
net realized gains on the TMCT&nbsp;I Portfolio of $1&nbsp;million, $4&nbsp;million and $2&nbsp;million, respectively. The net realized gains were recorded as non-operating items
in each year. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company and the Chandler Trusts share in the cash flows of the various assets held by TMCT&nbsp;II. The cash flows from the REIT Portfolio, the
TMCT&nbsp;II Portfolio and the Venture Capital Portfolio are largely allocated to the Chandler Trusts. The cash flows from the TMCT&nbsp;II Shares are largely allocated to the Company. Due to the
allocations of the economic benefits in TMCT&nbsp;II, for financial reporting purposes 80% of the TMCT&nbsp;II Shares are included in treasury stock, 80% of the preferred stock dividends on the
Series&nbsp;D-1 and D-2 preferred stock are excluded from preferred stock dividends and 80% of the dividends on the common stock are effectively eliminated. The Company
accounts for its 20% investments in the REIT Portfolio, the TMCT&nbsp;II Portfolio and the Venture Capital Portfolio under the equity method. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company's investment in TMCT&nbsp;II totaled $196&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and $198&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004 and Dec.&nbsp;28, 2003. The Company
recognized equity income related to the REIT Portfolio, TMCT&nbsp;II Portfolio and Venture Capital Portfolio investments of $8&nbsp;million in 2005, $9&nbsp;million in 2004 and
$10&nbsp;million in 2003. During 2005, 2004 and 2003, the Company recorded net losses of $3&nbsp;million, $4&nbsp;million and $8&nbsp;million, respectively, related to net realized losses and
the write-downs of certain investments in the Venture Capital Portfolio. The net losses were recorded as non-operating items in each year. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
TMCT&nbsp;I and TMCT&nbsp;II LLC agreements have no specific term, and the dissolution, determination of liquidation values and distribution of assets require the mutual consent
of the Company and the Chandler Trusts. </FONT></P>

<A NAME="page_fo1126_1_89"> </A>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT SIZE=2><B>Long-Term Debt Issuance&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In 2005, the Company issued $450&nbsp;million
($449&nbsp;million net of unamortized discount) 4.875% notes due 2010 and $330&nbsp;million ($328&nbsp;million net of unamortized discount) 5.25% notes due 2015. The proceeds from the issuance
were used to repay commercial paper. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Medium-Term Notes&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Notes issued under these programs generally have maturities from one to six years and may not be
redeemed by the Company prior to maturity. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Interest Rate Swap</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>&#151;The Company is currently a party to one interest rate swap agreement. This swap agreement relates to the
$100&nbsp;million 7.5% debentures due in 2023 and effectively converts the fixed 7.5% rate to a variable rate based on LIBOR. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Current Portion of Long-Term Debt&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The current portion of long-term debt at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005
includes $286&nbsp;million of commercial paper, $15&nbsp;million of property financing obligation and $2&nbsp;million of other obligations due within one year. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Exchangeable Subordinated Debentures due 2029 ("PHONES")&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In 1999, the Company issued 8&nbsp;million PHONES for an aggregate
principal amount of approximately $1.3&nbsp;billion. The principal amount was equal to the value of 16&nbsp;million shares of Time Warner common stock at the closing price of $78.50 per share on
April&nbsp;7, 1999. Quarterly interest payments are made to the PHONES holders at an annual rate of 2% of the initial principal. The Company records both cash and non-cash interest
expense on the discounted debt component of the PHONES. The PHONES debenture agreement requires principal payments equal to any dividends declared on the 16&nbsp;million shares of Time Warner common
stock. In 2005, Time Warner declared quarterly dividends of $.05 per share. A payment of $.10 per PHONES was made in the fourth quarter of 2005, and a payment of $.10 per PHONES will be due in the
first quarter of 2006. The company records the dividends it receives on its Time Warner common stock as dividend income and accounts for the related payment to the PHONES holders as principal
reduction. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company may redeem the PHONES at any time for the higher of the principal value of the PHONES ($156.84 per PHONES at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005) or the then market value of two shares of
Time Warner common stock, subject to certain adjustments. At any time, holders of the PHONES may exchange a PHONES for an amount of cash equal to 95% (or 100% under certain circumstances) of the
market value of two shares of Time Warner common stock. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the market value per PHONES was $74.00, and the market value of two shares of Time Warner common stock was $35.36. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under
the provisions of FAS No.&nbsp;133, the PHONES consist of a discounted debt component, which is presented at book value, and a derivative component, which is presented at fair
value. Changes in the fair value of the derivative component of the PHONES are recorded in the statement of income. The fair value of the derivative component of the PHONES debt is calculated as the
difference between the quoted market value of the PHONES and the estimated fair value of the discounted debt component of the PHONES. The fair value of the discounted debt component of the PHONES is
calculated based on an estimate of the current interest rate available to the Company for debt of the same remaining maturity and similar terms to the PHONES. The book value of the discounted debt
component is based on the prevailing interest rate (8.125%) at issuance of the PHONES. The market value of the PHONES, which are traded on the New York Stock Exchange, was $592&nbsp;million and
$728&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, respectively. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If the PHONES are exchanged in the next year, the Company intends to refinance the PHONES, and has the ability to do so on a long-term basis through
its existing revolving credit agreements. Accordingly, the PHONES have been classified as long-term. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Revolving Credit Agreements&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the Company had revolving credit agreements with a number of financial
institutions providing for borrowings in an aggregate amount of up to $1.2&nbsp;billion. Borrowings under these agreements, which expire in December&nbsp;2008, would be at a rate equal to LIBOR
plus 0.35%. The revolving credit agreements allow the Company to elect one-month to twelve-month LIBOR rates, based on the term of the borrowing. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the
one-month LIBOR rate was 4.38% and the twelve-month LIBOR rate was 4.85%. The agreements contain various interest rate options and provide for annual fees based on a percentage of the
commitment. The agreements contain covenants that require the Company to maintain a minimum interest coverage ratio. No amounts were borrowed under the agreements at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, and the
Company was in compliance with the covenants. Annual fees totaled approximately $1.1&nbsp;million in 2005, $0.9&nbsp;million in 2004 and $1.1&nbsp;million in 2003. In addition to the exchange
value of the PHONES, the Company intends to refinance $638&nbsp;million of commercial paper and $293&nbsp;million of medium-term notes scheduled to mature by Dec.&nbsp;25, 2006, and
has the ability to do so on a long-term basis through its existing revolving credit agreements. Accordingly, these notes and commercial paper have been classified as long-term. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The following methods and assumptions were used to estimate the fair value of each category of financial instruments. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Cost Method Investments&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Cost method investments in public companies were recorded at fair value in the consolidated balance
sheets (see Notes&nbsp;1 and 7). Cost method investments in private companies were recorded at cost, net of write-downs, and fair value was generally estimated based on prices recently paid for
shares in those companies. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Debt&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Fair value was estimated based on quoted market prices for similar issues or on current rates available to the Company
for debt of the same remaining maturities and similar terms. The carrying value of the Company's derivative instruments approximates fair value. The fair value of the PHONES was determined by
reference to the market value resulting from trading on a national securities exchange. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Contracts Payable for Broadcast Rights&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Fair value was estimated using the discounted cash flow method. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT SIZE=2><B>Operating Loss Carryforwards&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the Company had approximately
$676&nbsp;million of operating loss carryforwards for state income tax purposes. These carryforwards arose in certain states primarily as a result of intercompany interest expense, royalty expense
and management fees allocated to the Company's various subsidiaries, and expire between 2006 and 2025. The deferred tax assets related to these carryforwards totaled approximately $34&nbsp;million,
net of federal taxes, at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005. However, the Company believes it is more likely than not that $30&nbsp;million of the deferred tax assets will not be realized because the related
carryforwards will expire before being utilized. Therefore, in accordance with FAS No.&nbsp;109, "Accounting for Income Taxes," the Company has established valuation allowances of $30&nbsp;million
on the deferred tax assets related to the state carryforwards. The state operating loss carryforwards increased in 2005 because the Company generated additional tax losses in certain states. </FONT></P>

<!-- ZEQ.=2,SEQ=96,EFW="2167668",CP="TRIBUNE CO.",DN="1",CHK=32731,FOLIO='93',FILE='DISK131:[06CHI6.06CHI1126]FQ1126A.;17',USER='SLYUBOM',CD='27-FEB-2006;16:00' -->
<A NAME="page_fq1126_1_94"> </A>
<BR>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Matthew Bender and Mosby Tax Liability&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>During 1998, Times Mirror, which was acquired by the Company in 2000, disposed of its
Matthew Bender and Mosby subsidiaries in separate transactions, which were structured to qualify as tax-free reorganizations under the Internal Revenue Code. The Company believes these
transactions were completed on a tax-free basis. However, the Internal Revenue Service ("IRS") audited the transactions and disagreed with the position taken by Times Mirror. In the fourth
quarter of 2001, the Company
received an IRS adjustment to increase Times Mirror's 1998 taxable income by approximately $1.6&nbsp;billion. The Company filed a petition in United States Tax Court in November&nbsp;2002 to
contest the IRS position, and in December&nbsp;2004, the Company presented its position in United States Tax Court. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On
Sept.&nbsp;27, 2005, the United States Tax Court issued an opinion contrary to the Company's position and determined that the Matthew Bender transaction was a taxable sale. In
January&nbsp;2006, the Tax Court extended its opinion in the Matthew Bender case to the Mosby transaction given the similarity of the two transactions. Taxes and related interest for both the
Matthew Bender and Mosby transactions total approximately $1&nbsp;billion. Over time, deductions for state taxes and interest are expected to reduce the net cash outlay to approximately
$840&nbsp;million. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company will appeal the Tax Court ruling to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. The Company does not expect a ruling before the first half of 2007. The
Company cannot predict with certainty the outcome of this appeal. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Times
Mirror established a tax reserve of $180&nbsp;million in 1998 when it entered into the transactions. The reserve represented Times Mirror's best estimate of the amount the
expected IRS and state income tax claims could be settled for based upon an analysis of the facts and circumstances surrounding the issue. In accordance with Emerging Issues Task Force ("EITF") Issue
No.&nbsp;93-7, "Uncertainties Related to Income Taxes in a Purchase Business Combination," the Company treated this item as an uncertain tax position at the time of the Times Mirror
acquisition in 2000 and concluded that the estimate determined by Times Mirror was the most appropriate estimate of the exposure. The Company has maintained this initial reserve, plus interest, and
has evaluated the adequacy of the reserve on a periodic basis. At Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, the reserve, including pretax interest of $66&nbsp;million, totaled $246&nbsp;million ($221&nbsp;million
after including the tax benefit of the interest). In 2005, prior to the Tax Court ruling, the Company recorded additional after-tax interest of $7&nbsp;million on the reserve. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As
a result of the Tax Court ruling, the Company increased its tax reserve by an additional $609&nbsp;million in the third quarter of 2005 by recording additional income tax expense of
$150&nbsp;million, representing additional after-tax interest applicable to the post-acquisition period, and goodwill of $459&nbsp;million. In accordance with EITF
No.&nbsp;93-7, the Company adjusted goodwill because the tax contingencies existed at the time of the Times Mirror acquisition. On Sept.&nbsp;30, 2005, the Company paid
$880&nbsp;million to the IRS, representing the federal tax and interest owed on the transactions, and financed the payment through the issuance of commercial paper. The Company expects to make
related state tax and interest payments of approximately $125&nbsp;million during 2006 ($87&nbsp;million after including the federal tax benefit of the state taxes and interest). </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT SIZE=2><B>PHONES&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In connection with the routine examination of the Company's federal income tax
returns for 2000 and 2001, the IRS has proposed that the Company capitalize the interest on the PHONES as additional tax basis in the Company's 16&nbsp;million shares of Time Warner common stock,
rather than currently deducting such interest. The National Office of the IRS has issued a Technical Advice Memorandum that supports the proposed treatment. The Company disagrees with the IRS's
position and requested that the IRS administrative appeals office review the issue. An appeals officer was appointed in August&nbsp;2005, and the Company had an initial meeting with the appeals
office in December&nbsp;2005. Discussions with the appeals office regarding this issue are on-going. The effect of the treatment proposed by the IRS would be to increase the Company's
tax liability by approximately $88&nbsp;million for the period 2000-2001 and by approximately $214&nbsp;million for the period 2002 through 2005. If the IRS were to prevail in its
proposed treatment, there would be no effect on the Company's reported income for any of these periods. The potential tax payments would be recorded as a reduction in the Company's deferred tax
liability, and the Company has accrued the interest that would be assessed on these potential payments. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Income Tax Reserves&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company's liability for estimated federal and state audit adjustments, including after-tax
interest, was approximately $96&nbsp;million and $326&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, respectively. These amounts are included in "other obligations" in the
Company's consolidated balance sheet. The liability declined in 2005 primarily because of the United States Tax Court decision regarding the Matthew Bender transaction. As discussed in the "Matthew
Bender and Mosby Tax Liability" section above, the Company had an income tax reserve of $221&nbsp;million at Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004 for this issue. During the third quarter of 2005, the tax reserve
was reclassified to "other current liabilities" in the Company's consolidated balance sheet. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Although
management believes its estimates and judgments are reasonable, the resolutions of the Company's tax issues are unpredictable and could result in tax liabilities that are
significantly higher or lower than that which has been provided by the Company. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>NOTE 13: PENSION AND POSTRETIREMENT BENEFITS</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT SIZE=2><B>Employee Pension Plans&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In connection with the establishment of the Tribune Company ESOP in 1988,
Tribune amended its company-sponsored pension plan for employees not covered by a collective bargaining agreement. The Tribune Company pension plan continued to provide substantially the same pension
benefits as under the pre-amended plan until December&nbsp;1998. After that date, Tribune pension benefit credits were frozen in terms of pay and service. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In
connection with the Times Mirror acquisition, the Company assumed defined benefit pension plans and various other contributory and non-contributory retirement plans
covering substantially all of Times Mirror's former employees. In general, benefits under the Times Mirror defined benefit plans were based on years of service and the employee's compensation during
the last five years of employment. In December&nbsp;2005, the pension plan benefits for former Times Mirror non-union and non-Newsday employees were frozen. As a result of
the plan freeze, a pretax curtailment gain of $18&nbsp;million was recorded. On March&nbsp;31, 2006, the pension plan benefits for Newsday union and non-union employees will be frozen.
Benefits provided by Times Mirror's Employee Stock Ownership Plan ("Times Mirror ESOP") are coordinated with certain pension benefits and, as a result, the defined benefit plan obligations are net of
the actuarially equivalent value of the benefits earned under the Times Mirror ESOP. The maximum offset is equal to the value of the benefits earned under the defined benefit plan. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The
Company also maintains several small plans for other employees. The Company's portion of assets and liabilities for multi-employer union pension plans is not determinable. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</FONT><FONT
SIZE=2><B>Postretirement Benefits Other Than Pensions&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company provides postretirement health care and life insurance benefits to
eligible employees under a variety of plans. The various plans have significantly different provisions for lifetime maximums, retiree cost-sharing, health care providers, prescription drug
coverage and other benefits. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><A
NAME="page_fs1126_1_99"> </A> </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company used a building block approach to determine its current 8.5% assumption of the long-term expected rate of return on pension plan assets.
Based on historical market studies, the Company's long-term expected returns for equity and fixed income securities approximate 10% and 6%, respectively. The Company's current 2006 target
asset allocation for pension plan assets is 75% in equity securities and 25% in fixed income securities and other. The Company bases the rate used for discounting future benefit obligations and
calculating interest cost on an index of Aa-rated corporate bonds. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At
Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005 and Dec.&nbsp;26, 2004, the Company's prepaid pension asset included an unrecognized net actuarial loss of $870&nbsp;million and $803&nbsp;million,
respectively. A significant portion of this net actuarial loss resulted from the difference between the Company's expected returns on plan assets and the actual losses on plan assets in 2002 and 2001.
Expected returns on plan assets were $158&nbsp;million and $176&nbsp;million in 2002 and 2001, respectively; actual losses were $161&nbsp;million and $113&nbsp;million, respectively. In
accordance with FAS No.&nbsp;87, "Employers' Accounting for Pensions," the actuarial loss will be recognized in net periodic pension expense over the estimated average remaining service period of
active employees expected to receive benefits. The Company's policy is to incorporate asset-related gains and losses into the asset value used to calculate the expected return on plan assets and into
the calculation of amortization of unrecognized net actuarial loss over a four-year period. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Health Care Cost Trend Rates&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>For purposes of measuring 2005 postretirement health care costs, a 9.0% annual rate of increase in the per
capita cost of covered health care benefits was assumed for 2005. The rate was assumed to decrease gradually to 5.0% for 2009 and remain at that level thereafter. For purposes of measuring health care
obligations at Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, a 9.0% annual rate of increase in the per capita cost of covered health care benefits was assumed for 2005. The rate was assumed to decrease gradually to 5.0% for
2010 and remain at that level thereafter. On Dec.&nbsp;8, 2003, the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement and Modernization Act of 2003 ("Act") was signed into law. The Act resulted in a
$15&nbsp;million reduction in the accumulated other postretirement obligations for prior service costs and a $1&nbsp;million reduction in net periodic postretirement benefit costs. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Assumed

rates would have the following effects (in thousands): </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>NOTE 14: CAPITAL STOCK AND SHARE PURCHASE PLAN</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the Company's Restated Certificate of Incorporation, 12&nbsp;million shares of preferred stock are authorized. Preferred stock is issuable in series under
terms and conditions determined by the Company's Board of Directors. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Series&nbsp;B Preferred Stock&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In 1989, the Company established a series of 1.6&nbsp;million shares of Series&nbsp;B Convertible
Preferred Stock and issued 1.59&nbsp;million shares to the Company's ESOP. In December&nbsp;2003, the Series&nbsp;B convertible preferred stock was converted into 15.4&nbsp;million shares of
common stock. Each share of the Series&nbsp;B preferred stock paid a cumulative dividend of 7.75% annually, had a liquidation value of $220 per share, was convertible into 16 shares of the Company's
common stock and was voted with the common stock with an entitlement to 18.32 votes per preferred share. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Series&nbsp;C, D-1 and D-2 Convertible Preferred Stock&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In connection with the June&nbsp;12, 2000 merger with
Times Mirror, outstanding shares of Times Mirror cumulative, non-voting preferred stock were converted into shares of Tribune preferred stock with similar terms. An additional
0.2&nbsp;million shares of preferred stock, net of treasury stock, were issued due to the conversion. Series&nbsp;C convertible preferred stock is cumulative, non-voting preferred
stock, which is entitled to annual dividends of 8%, based on liquidation value. Annual dividends for Series&nbsp;D-1 and D-2 were paid at the rate of 6.67%, 6.44% and 6.22%
in 2005, 2004, and 2003, respectively, and will be paid at the rate of 6.91% in 2006 based on liquidation value. Dividends on Series&nbsp;D-1 and D-2 preferred stocks will
increase ratably from 2006 until 2012 pursuant to a predetermined schedule. Series&nbsp;C, D-1 and D-2 convertible preferred stocks relate to Times Mirror recapitalization
transactions whereby TMCT&nbsp;I and TMCT&nbsp;II (see Note&nbsp;6) were formed. Series&nbsp;C, D-1 and D-2 preferred stocks are convertible into the Company's common
stock in 2025 and thereafter. The conversion factor is calculated by dividing $500 plus accrued and unpaid dividends by the average closing prices of the Company's common stock for the 20 trading days
immediately preceding the conversion date. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Common and Treasury Stock&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>At Feb.&nbsp;17, 2006, there were 6,461 holders of record. During 2005, the Company repurchased and retired
12.2&nbsp;million shares of its common stock in the open market for $440&nbsp;million. During 2004, the Company repurchased and retired 15.5&nbsp;million shares of its common stock in the open
market for $732&nbsp;million. During 2003, the Company repurchased 7.5&nbsp;million shares of </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Treasury Common Stock Held by Tribune Stock Compensation Fund ("TSCF")&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The TSCF purchased shares of the Company's common stock for the

Company's common stock for $20&nbsp;million. All shares acquired in 2003 by TSCF were utilized by December&nbsp;2003. The TSCF was dissolved in the first quarter of 2005. </FONT></P>


<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Share Purchase Rights Plan&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In December&nbsp;1997, the Company adopted a Share Purchase Rights Plan that replaced a similar agreement. The
plan provides for a dividend of one right on each outstanding share of the Company's common stock. Each right will entitle stockholders to buy one two-hundredth of a share of
Series&nbsp;A Junior Participating preferred stock at an exercise price of $125. These rights expire Jan.&nbsp;5, 2008. The rights have no voting rights and are not exercisable until
10&nbsp;days after the occurrence of certain triggering events, upon which the holders of the rights are entitled to purchase either the common stock of an acquirer or additional common stock of the
Company at a discounted price. The rights are redeemable at the option of the Company for $.005 per right. The Company has established a series of two&nbsp;million shares of Series&nbsp;A Junior
Participating Preferred Stock in connection with the plan, none of which have been issued. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>NOTE 15: INCENTIVE COMPENSATION AND STOCK PLANS</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Defined Contribution Plans&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company maintains various qualified 401(k) savings plans, which permit eligible employees to make voluntary
contributions on a pretax basis. The plans allow participants to invest their savings in various investments including the Company's common stock. The Company enhanced its primary 401(k) plan to
include a larger Company contribution in 2004. This new plan was designed to replace the Company's ESOP that was fully allocated at the end of 2003. Company contributions to all of its defined
contribution plans were $33&nbsp;million in 2005, $32&nbsp;million in 2004 and $17&nbsp;million in 2003. In 2005, the Company contributed an additional $26&nbsp;million to these plans,
which related to and was charged to expense in 2004. In 2006, the Company will contribute to these plans an additional $26&nbsp;million, which relates to and was charged to expense in 2005. In 2006,
the Company amended its primary 401(k) plan to make a portion of the Company's contributions discretionary. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Employee Stock Purchase Plan&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>This plan permits eligible employees to purchase the Company's common stock at 85% of market price. The Company
incurred charges of $0.2&nbsp;million in 2005, 2004 and 2003 related to the administration of this plan. During 2005, 2004 and 2003, 682,624, 617,651, and 568,718 shares, respectively, were sold to
employees under this plan. A total of 16&nbsp;million shares can be purchased under this plan. As of Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, a total of 3.1&nbsp;million shares remained available for sale. The
weighted average fair value of shares sold in 2005 was $36.37. The Company plans to adopt FAS No.&nbsp;123R in the first quarter of 2006 (see Note&nbsp;1). FAS&nbsp;123R requires that the
discount on purchases of the Company's common stock provided to eligible employees under the plan be expensed. The Company expects to record approximately $3.7&nbsp;million of expense in 2006
related to the plan. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Employee Stock Ownership Plan ("ESOP")&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In 1988, the Company established an ESOP as a long-term employee benefit plan. In
connection therewith, the ESOP purchased, in 1988 and 1989, </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>1997 Incentive Compensation Plan&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>In 1997, the 1992 Long-Term Incentive Plan was replaced with the 1997 Incentive Compensation
Plan. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, remaining options outstanding under the 1992 plan totaled 60,000 shares, all of which were exercisable. The 1997 plan provides for the granting of awards to eligible
employees in any one or combination of stock options, performance equity program awards and annual management incentive program bonuses. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, options outstanding under the 1997
plan totaled 36.7&nbsp;million shares, of which 35.2&nbsp;million shares were exercisable. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, a total of 32.2&nbsp;million shares were available for award under the 1997
plan. The stock options assumed in the Times Mirror acquisition are fully vested and exercisable. At Dec.&nbsp;25, 2005, the converted Times Mirror stock options outstanding and exercisable totaled
7.2&nbsp;million shares. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under
the stock option portion of the 1997 plan, the option price may not be less than the market value of the Company's common stock at the time the option is granted. Options are
exercisable not less than six months or more than 10&nbsp;years after the date the option is granted. General awards granted under the 1997 plan vest in annual 25% increments beginning one year from
the date of the grant. Under certain circumstances, replacement options are granted when a participant pays the exercise price of a stock option and related tax withholding obligations with previously
acquired shares of common stock. The number of replacement options granted is equal to the number of shares used to pay the exercise price and related tax withholding obligations. The exercise price

<A NAME="page_fs1126_1_106"> </A>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B><U>NOTE 17: BUSINESS SEGMENTS</U>  </B></FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tribune Company is a media and entertainment company that conducts its operations through two business segments: publishing and broadcasting and entertainment. In
addition, certain administrative activities are reported and included under corporate. These segments reflect the manner in which the Company sells its products to the marketplace and the manner in
which it manages its operations and makes business decisions. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Publishing&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>Tribune Publishing operates 11 market-leading daily newspapers and related businesses, distributes entertainment listings and
syndicated content, operates a 24-hour cable news channel, and manages the websites of Tribune's daily newspapers and television stations, along with other branded sites targeting specific
communities of interest. The daily newspapers are the </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Los Angeles Times</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>; </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Chicago Tribune</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>; </FONT> <FONT SIZE=2><I>Newsday</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, serving
Nassau and Suffolk counties on Long Island, New York and the borough of Queens, New York; </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>South Florida
Sun-Sentinel; Orlando Sentinel</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>; </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>The Baltimore Sun</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>; </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>The Hartford Courant; The Morning
Call</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, serving Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley; </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Daily Press</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, serving the Virginia Peninsula; and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>The
Advocate</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2> and </FONT><FONT SIZE=2><I>Greenwich Time</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>, each serving Connecticut's Fairfield County. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2><B>Broadcasting and Entertainment&#151;</B></FONT><FONT SIZE=2>The Company's broadcasting operations consist of The WB Television Network affiliates in New York, Los
Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, Boston, Dallas, Washington D.C., Atlanta, Houston, Seattle, Miami, Denver, St.&nbsp;Louis, Portland, Indianapolis, San Diego, Hartford, New Orleans, and Albany; FOX
television affiliates in Seattle, Sacramento, Indianapolis, Hartford, Grand Rapids and Harrisburg; an ABC television affiliate in New Orleans; and
one radio station in Chicago. On Jan.&nbsp;24, 2006, the Company announced that it had reached a 10-year agreement to affiliate 16 of its WB Network affiliates stations with a new
broadcast network, The CW Network, being launched in the fall of 2006. The WB Network will shut down at that time. Three of the Company's current WB Network affiliates (Philadelphia, Atlanta and
Seattle) will become independent stations at that time. Entertainment operations include Tribune Entertainment which distributes its own programming together with programming licensed from third
parties. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT SIZE=2>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;No
single customer provides more than 10% of the Company's revenue. In determining operating profit for each segment, none of the following items have been added or deducted: interest
and dividend income, interest expense, equity income and loss, non-operating items or income taxes. Assets represent those tangible and intangible assets used in the operations of each
segment. Corporate assets include cash and the Company's investment portfolio. </FONT></P>

impact in the first quarter, increase of $.12 in second quarter, increase of $.05 in the third quarter and decrease of $.05 in the fourth quarter. For 2004 by quarter, the effect on diluted EPS was as
follows: decrease of $.09 in the first quarter, increase of $.04 in second quarter, decrease of $.04 in the third quarter and increase of $.06 in the fourth quarter.
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='margin-bottom:-9pt;'><FONT SIZE=1>(2)</FONT></DT><DD><FONT SIZE=1>During
2005 and 2004, the Company sold certain subsidiaries and investments. For 2005, the gain on sales of subsidiaries and investments resulted in the pretax gain of
$7&nbsp;million in the aggregate, increasing diluted EPS by $.01. For 2004, the gain on sales of subsidiaries and investments related primarily to the sale of the Company's 50% interest in </FONT> <FONT SIZE=1><I>La Opini&oacute;n</I></FONT><FONT
SIZE=1>. The sale of </FONT><FONT SIZE=1><I>La Opini&oacute;n</I></FONT><FONT SIZE=1> resulted in a pretax gain of
$18&nbsp;million, increasing diluted EPS by $.03 in the first quarter of 2004.

2004, the Company recorded investment write-downs, which in the aggregate, decreased full year pretax income by $6&nbsp;million and diluted EPS by $.01. For 2004 by quarter,

other intangible assets are no longer amortized to earnings.
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='margin-bottom:-9pt;'><FONT SIZE=1>(2)</FONT></DT><DD><FONT SIZE=1>During
the second quarter of 2001, the Company announced a voluntary employee retirement program. The Company implemented this program as well as various other cost reduction
initiatives throughout the remainder of 2001 and the first quarter of 2002. In the aggregate, the restructuring charges related to these programs decreased 2002 full year net income by
$17&nbsp;million and diluted EPS by $.05 and decreased 2001 full year net income by $93&nbsp;million and diluted EPS by $.29.
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='margin-bottom:-9pt;'><FONT SIZE=1>(3)</FONT></DT><DD><FONT SIZE=1>The
cumulative effect of adopting a new accounting pronouncement for the valuation of certain intangible assets decreased net income by $18&nbsp;million in 2004. The cumulative
effect of adopting a new accounting pronouncement for goodwill and other intangible assets decreased net income by $166&nbsp;million in 2002. The cumulative effect of adopting a new accounting
pronouncement for derivative instruments decreased net income by $3&nbsp;million in 1999.
<BR><BR></FONT></DD><DT style='margin-bottom:-9pt;'><FONT SIZE=1>(4)</FONT></DT><DD><FONT SIZE=1>Includes

as a result of the Matthew Bender Tax Court ruling, partially offset by $12&nbsp;million of favorable income tax settlement adjustments), totaling a loss of $96&nbsp;million, or $.30 per diluted
share, in 2005; loss on changes in fair values of derivatives and related investments of $11&nbsp;million, loss on early debt retirement of $87&nbsp;million, gain on sales of subsidiaries and
